body:
DESIGN-STAGE. The deliverable is a WORKING SPEC at `.adlc/specs/31-container-console.md` — criteria-bearing, gateable, `spec-lint --llm` clean — plus a reasoned recommendation on every question below. **Then STOP and wait for Myk's word in chat before any implementation code.** No prose goes into `spec/` until the landing PR.

ORIGIN (Myk, 2026-07-25, in chat), in his words: *"a web interface for containers. A user logs in and they see their root container. If this user is also the operator, they can also see the whole store-as-container. But anyone can also step into any container within their user container, and perform any operations over it. They can see offered federations waiting on policies, they can see (and mutate!) existing federations, they can promote anything up, they can drop quarantines."*

WHY IT IS ONE INTERFACE AND NOT FIVE. Store browser, quarantine manager, federation console, promotion review, module installer — every one of them is an OPERATION ON A CONTAINER, so one navigable surface subsumes all five and the abstraction pays for itself instead of being described. It is also the first thing that makes containers visible to anyone who has not read §27 and §28. That is the argument for building it: not a feature, a demonstration that the primitive is real.

FRAME IT AS T79'S SECOND ARM WITH A PURPOSE, and do not re-litigate the seam. §23.2 promised a stock React host whose router is derived from the store; T79's working spec (`.adlc/specs/30-renderer-dual-target.md`) says plainly that no React exists anywhere in `src/`, builds the ARTIFACT arm first, and builds it precisely so the client-host seam is paid for once — *"the React host becomes a swap of the data client"*. It also names the shared FLOOR exactly: a pure synchronous `RenderFn`, a `RenderNode` of `{ entity, view, hex, reads, state }`, `_view` as the projection on every read, `data-loam-read` and `<form>` gestures naming a lens and an entity, a host-neutral four-code refusal vocabulary, and the app's SCHEMA as the request surface. T79's own table names what is ABOVE the floor and differs per surface (`window.claude.mcp` vs `fetch`/SSE, poll vs stream, one page vs a derived router). The console is the second deploy surface standing on that floor. Reuse it; the spec's job is to say which floor members it needs and which above-floor affordances it requires, not to invent a new runtime.

THE SPEC MUST ANSWER THESE FIVE, WITH ARGUMENTS RATHER THAN ASSERTIONS.

**1. THE TENANCY FORK — this is the whole design, and everything else is downstream of it.** Verified in the tree: reads are IDENTITY-INDEPENDENT within a mount. `gqlHooks` passes `resolve: (name, entity, asOf)` with no actor at all (`src/gateway/gateway.ts:404`), while every mutation takes an `actorSeed` (`:405-414`); the HTTP layer turns a token into an identity and threads it ONLY into writes and two operator-gated doors (`src/server/http.ts:295`, `:895`). The only read-side discrimination that exists is the full-door / public-door split (`Gateway.surface(door)`), which is per-token-CLASS, never per-actor. So: **one user per store (or per mount) is buildable today, with real isolation, because the isolation is the mount rather than a lens.** Many users in one store needs the read-side capability slice §24.2 deferred, and that slice does not exist in any form.

   RECOMMEND THE FIRST, and say what the second costs — but state the constraint accurately, because the framing this ticket was raised with overstates it. §27.8's DECIDED invariant is *"any delta ingested into your store is visible to you ... 'internal' means NOT-ADVERTISED. It never means NOT-READABLE"*, and §27.8 states it AT THE STORE LEVEL, about the store's own OPERATOR: *"a store has no compartments hidden from its own operator."* The same passage then says what a future read-side slice may be: it *"can only ever govern what a door serves to OTHERS, never what an operator sees in their own store"*, and rules out only designs that read as *"hide these deltas from the store that holds them."* So many-users-in-one-store is BOUNDED by the invariant, not forbidden by it — non-operator users are exactly the "others" a door may narrow for. What IS forbidden head-on is the console's own sketch pushed one step too far: a seat that can "step into any container and perform any operation over it" is an operator-shaped seat, and N operator-shaped seats in one store is N readers from whom nothing is hidden. That is the contradiction, and it is with the SKETCH rather than with multi-tenancy.

   So the honest cost of many-users-in-one-store, to be written down: (a) a read-side door narrowing that does not exist and whose absence is total — there is no per-actor read path to extend; (b) a promise weaker than the mount gives, since §27.8 caps it at what a DOOR serves and any direct `select`/`freeze`/`offeredDeltas` caller bypasses it; and (c) it lands on the surface §24.2 deferred and §7's seam already noticed. One-user-per-store costs a mount per user and buys mount-level isolation that is already built and already tested (T78).

**2. TWO OF THE SKETCH'S VERBS ARE OPERATOR-ONLY BY DESIGN, NOT BY OMISSION.** Do not invent a delegation to cover them; say so. Verified: promotion re-signs in the OPERATOR's voice — §24.3's adoption-merge and `adoptLaw` refuse outright without an operator seed (`src/gateway/adopt-law.ts:1050`) and record provenance under `gw.operatorAuthor`. Erasure is the operator's alone and the store is deliberately unforgiving about it: *"erasure is the instance operator's alone: only the operator may order a record removed"* (`src/gateway/erase.ts:115`), enforced at BOTH doors. And "drop a quarantine" is an erasure by construction — `Container.drop()` purges the wall's bytes and verifies at the bytes, and `openWall` refuses at all without the primary's operator seed (`src/gateway/container.ts:854`). So a non-operator seat that drops a quarantine is a non-operator performing an erasure, which is the one authority §28.5 names as un-delegable (*"I can forget, and I cap the bill"*).

   Under one-store-per-user this is MOOT — the user IS their store's operator — which is a second, independent argument for recommendation 1. Write it that way: the tenancy fork is not only about reads; it is what makes three of Myk's five verbs expressible at all.

**3. A USER'S CONTAINER IS A VIEW KEYED ON AN AUTHOR, NOT THE AUTHOR ITSELF.** A property-posture container with membership `{"op":"select","pred":{"match":{"field":"author","cmp":"eq","const":"<author>"}},"in":"input"}` — note the posture is `property`, not `shared` (there is no `shared` posture; §27.1's vocabulary is `wall | property`). This is the better model because "my drafts" and "my team's stuff" then become the SAME KIND OF OBJECT, differing only in the predicate — one navigation model, one set of operations, no special case for "me". The spec's navigation model must reflect that: the console navigates the containment tree (§28.8's forest, `parent` edges, `readContainerTable`), and a user's home is one node in it rather than a distinguished frame. Two consequences to state: a property container is a QUERY, so "my container" re-evaluates live as the ground grows and nothing needs to be moved into it; and a membership Term is latest-wins per §27.1, so redefining "mine" is a delta.

**4. "FEDERATIONS WAITING ON POLICIES" IS NEW VOCABULARY AND THE BEST PART OF THE SKETCH.** Verified: federation today has exactly two shapes and neither is an offer awaiting a decision. PULL is `pullFrom(gateway, url, token)` — one anti-entropy step the local store initiates (`src/federation/pull.ts:44`). PUSH is `federate(deltas, { admit })` — the receiver applies a predicate per delta and admits or rejects on the spot (`src/gateway/ingest.ts:290`), with `admitForImpl` resolving the store's `loam:trust` policy when no predicate is given. There is no PENDING state anywhere: a delta is admitted or it is rejected and counted, and `FederationReport` is `{ offered, accepted, rejected }`. So this is genuinely new design, and it is the piece that turns the trust model from something you CONFIGURE into something you DO.

   The spec must name, with arguments: (a) WHAT A PENDING OFFER IS AT REST — a new `loam.*` context following the `loam:trust`/`loam.container*` precedent (a declaration resolved live from deltas, so a decision is a delta and never a restart), and critically whether the offered DELTAS are held (which is ingestion, and ingestion is visibility per §27.8 — so holding them means they are already readable and "pending" governs only what BINDS, not what is present) or merely DESCRIBED by address and count (which keeps the door closed but makes the offer un-inspectable, since content addresses resolve to nothing locally). (b) WHO MAY ACCEPT ONE — and this inherits §28.6's admission axis, which is where the honest answer already lives. (c) WHAT EXPIRY IT HAS, if any, in a grow-only store where nothing decays and a "pending" claim left standing forever is a claim about the present made in the past.

   And note the existing seam it should ride rather than parallel: §28.6's ADMISSION axis is already specified and already implemented as a reader — `containerAdmission(reactor, operator, container)` is `readTrustPolicyAt` filed at the container's entity (`src/gateway/container.ts:514`). It is called by NOTHING in `src/` (only `src/index.ts`'s re-export and two test files), so container-scoped admission is today a readable declaration that no door consults. An inbox whose accept-decision resolves through THAT policy makes both halves real at once; an inbox with its own private notion of who may accept forks the trust model.

**5. EVERY CRITERION NAMES ITS VERIFICATION** — a test path or a backtick command — or `spec-lint` fails it, which is the point (a criterion with no method is a wish). Two mechanical notes learned the hard way: a nested sub-bullet under a criterion LINTS AS ITS OWN CRITERION, so keep sub-points inline as (a)/(b)/(c) exactly as this ticket does; and prefer `--llm`/`--prompt-only`, which catches a method that is present but vacuous where the plain run only catches a missing one.

ALSO WORTH DECIDING IN THE SPEC, since the sketch implies them: which door the console speaks through (it is a full-door surface by nature — it shows quarantines and federation state, and §17's anonymous door answers a uniform 404 precisely so nothing leaks); whether it is served per-mount or above the mount table (T78's `MountTable` resolves static, dynamic, and attached-container mounts, and "step into a container" is exactly a mount traversal); and how it degrades when a container it names is unattached — `containerScope` and `openContainer` both FAIL CLOSED on an unreachable wall, and a console must render that refusal as a legible state rather than a blank panel (T79's `server_not_connected`/`upstream_error` precedent).

CARE: DESIGN-STAGE, therefore **Myk's merge (P6)**, and it never self-merges. It decides what a seat may do, which is the trust model. Expect the working spec to be long and expect question 1 to be answered before the others are worth writing.

OVERTAKEN (stale sweep, 2026-08-25): The console landed as §40 the admin page (T141, PR #330, src/server/admin.ts): a user logs in, sees their root container, walks the subtree, declares/detaches/drops containers, promotes, pastes federation offers, and revokes connections — extended by #451/#453/#454 (channel health, contested names, grant ledger). Its design questions were answered elsewhere too: §36 decided the tenancy fork (many users in one store, door-enforced subtree scope), §46 dissolved the 'no pending-offer vocabulary' premise, and §40.1 explicitly decided the operator's whole-store view goes to the CLI rather than the page.
title: The container console — a web interface where the container abstraction becomes something you DO
